title: Chapter 65: Breathing the Dead, Part 2 of 5: The Funeral Hour
html:
She worked it out by the sun.
It was not hard. She had learned the hours as a child, in the schoolroom at Crown Walk, from a governess with a long nose who believed that a lady ought to know how to tell the time without a watch, in case she was ever lost in the country. Lyra had thought it was the stupidest lesson in the world. She had sat at the window with her chin in her hand and watched the shadow of the garden wall creep across the lawn and said, "I will never, ever be lost in the country."
Now she stood at the south edge of Last Thorn and watched the shadow of a tent pole creep across the gravel, and thought, Miss Penhallow, you were right, and I hope you never find out.
Noon was easy. Noon was when the shadow of the pole was shortest, and pointed straight north, toward the ridge and the Glass. She had marked it with a stone. Then she had waited. The second bell after noon, in the city, was two hours past that. In winter, this far north, the sun moved fast and low across the south, and two hours was a long way along the sky. She had held her hand out at arm's length, the way Miss Penhallow had shown her, with the fingers together and the thumb tucked in, and measured. One hand from the top of the hills was the afternoon getting on. Two hands was the middle of it. She had worked it out three times to be sure, and then she had stopped working it out, because she knew. She could feel it coming, the way you feel the top of a stair coming in the dark.
The camp was busy behind her.
It had been busy all day. Busy in a different way from the morning. People were coming and going with armfuls of thorn wood from the slope and piling it on the big fire in the middle of the camp, more than they could need for cooking, much more, until the heap of it was taller than a man. Women were sitting outside the tents grinding something in stone bowls, a brown dry herb that smelled, when the wind brought it, of burnt honey. Children were being sent off on errands and coming back with things. Bone charms. Little clay pots. Bundles of hide. Nobody had explained any of it to her. But she knew what it was for.
Tonight.
She did not think about tonight. She did not have room to.
She stood at the south edge of the camp, where the last tent was, and the thorns began again, and the long slope went up and away toward the Lip. There was a flat place there, a little shelf of bare gravel between two thorn bushes, where you could stand and look south over the slope and see the line of the Lip against the sky, and beyond it, faint and blue and far away, the tops of the hills they had crossed.
South. The valleys were that way. Haverstock. Thistle Ford. Then the fens. Then the river. Then the dyke road, and the gates, and the city.
The Hill.
Saint Clement's on the Hill.
She had been there once a year, every year, all her life, until this one. At the turn of the year, for the service. In a new coat, with Rowan beside her in a new coat, and her father in front of them in his black coat with the silver buttons, and the bell going slow and the snow on the steps, and the smell of cold wax and wet wool inside. And saints painted on the walls with faded gold round their heads. She used to count them. Twenty-two saints. Twenty-three if you counted the little one over the door, which Rowan said did not count because it was only a head.
And under the church, down the crypt stair, the Thorne vault. She had been down there once. When she was small. Her father had taken her down, holding her hand, by lantern light, to show her where her grandmother was. Low arches and stone shelves and old long boxes and the smell of cold dust. And the tree with the crown in its branches cut into the stone over the door. She had been frightened. She had held his hand very tight. And he had said...
She did not remember what he had said.
She had burned it. Or it had gone some other way. She did not know which. She only knew that there had been something, there, in the dark, in the vault, that he had said to her to make her not afraid, and she did not have it anymore.
Today they were putting him down there.
In the box. On the shelf. Beside her mother.
And she was not there.
She stood on the little shelf of gravel and faced south. Her hands were at her sides. She had taken her gloves off without knowing she had done it, and they were in her coat pocket, and her bare hands were cold, and she let them be cold.
The sun went down the sky.
She watched it go. One hand from the hills. Less than one. She did not need to measure anymore. She knew.
And she thought: now.
Now the bell is going. Slow. One stroke and a long wait and another. Now the doors are open and the cold is coming in. Now they are carrying him up the aisle, on their shoulders, six of them, under the black cloth. Now the priest is saying the words. The long room where nothing is forgotten. Now Rowan is standing in the front pew in his cadet black with his chin up, the way Father taught him, not crying, because a Thorne does not cry in church.
Rowan.
Rowan, alone in the front pew. With nobody beside him.
She had not thought of that. Until this moment, she had not let herself think of it. That he would be there by himself. That she had left him there. That he would stand there in the front pew with the place beside him empty, and know exactly who was supposed to be standing in it, and that she was not.
She put her hand over her mouth.
She did not cry. She did not let herself. She stood there with her bare hand pressed hard over her mouth and her eyes wide open, staring south at the line of the Lip against the pale sky, and she did not cry, because a Thorne did not cry at a funeral, and because if she started she did not know how she would ever stop.
Behind her, on the gravel, something crunched.
She did not turn round. She knew the sound. A step, and the crutch, and a step. Slow, and uneven, and careful in the loose stones.
It stopped beside her.
He did not say anything. He did not touch her. He only came and stood beside her on the little gravel shelf, on her left, a little behind, leaning on his crutch, and faced the way she was facing.
South.
And they stood there together, the two of them, at the edge of the thorns, at the end of the world, with their backs to the Glass, at the second bell after noon.
Neither of them said anything for a long time.
She could feel the warmth of the Glass on the back of her neck. The dry steady prickle of it. The feeling of something standing behind her, close, looking. Arran had said you should never turn your back on it. Not ever.
She did not care.
Today she was looking south.
Like the Sea in a Harbor
"There's a room," she said at last.
She had not meant to say it. It came out on its own, in a small flat voice, to the hills.
"At Crown Walk. On the first floor. His study." She did not look at Corin. "Books on three of the walls. Up to the ceiling. And green curtains, velvet, that he never drew, even at night, because he liked to see the lamps in the street. And a desk by the window, a big one, with a crack in the top that he said his grandfather made with a sword, though I think he made it up."
The wind moved the thorns. Somewhere behind them in the camp a child laughed.
"And a lamp on the desk," said Lyra. "Brass. With a green shade. When it was lit, the whole desk went green, and his hands went green, and the papers. Like being under water. I used to sit under the desk when I was small. In the green. And he'd work, up above, and I'd sit by his feet, and he never once told me to go away."
She stopped. Her voice had gone.
Corin did not say anything. He waited.
"And the clock," she said, when she could. "A tall one, in the corner. With a moon on its face. A painted moon that went round, slowly, through the month, so you could see if it was full or new. And at night when the house was quiet you could hear it ticking from all the way up the stairs. I used to count the ticks. Going up to bed." She swallowed. "He's not there now. Nobody's there. It's all shut up. The curtains. And the lamp's out. And nobody's winding the clock."
She put her bare hands together in front of her, and pressed them, hard.
"It'll have stopped by now," she said. "The clock. It'll have run down. And nobody will know what time it stopped at."
The sun went down a little further.
And Corin said, beside her, very quietly:
"I know."
She turned her head.
He was not looking at her. He was looking south, the way she had been, at the Lip and the blue hills. His face was very still.
"I know the room," he said. "I've been in it."
She stared at him. "You've never been to Crown Walk."
"No." He shook his head slowly. "Not in my body. In his." A pause. "In his memory. When he was... before. When I walked it. I don't remember doing it. It's in the Ledger. But I remember the room." He frowned a little. "That's the strange part. I don't have walking it. But I've got the room. The way you've got a dream after you wake up. Some of it."
Lyra did not breathe.
"Two autumns ago," said Corin. "It was raining. You could hear it on the window. He was sitting in one of the leather chairs by the fire. Brown, both of them, and the arms worn pale where hands had rubbed them. There was a rug on the floor, red and blue, with a hole near the fender where a coal had jumped out once." He was quiet for a moment. "And the lamp was lit on the desk. Green. And the clock was going in the corner. And the moon on it was nearly full."
She could not speak.
"And he was thinking about you," said Corin.
The wind moved the thorns.
"I don't know what about," he said. "I don't have the thoughts. Just the feeling of them. He was sitting there in the green light with the rain on the window and he was thinking about you, and it..." He stopped. He seemed to be looking for a word. Then he found it, and he said it very simply, the way you say a thing you are sure of. "It felt like the sea in a harbor."
Lyra looked at him.
"Big," said Corin. "And quiet. And all the way round. You know. The way the sea is, inside a harbor wall, on a still night. Not going anywhere. Not doing anything. Just there. Holding all the boats up. All the way down, deeper than you can see." He turned his head and looked at her at last. "That's how he loved you. I felt it. That's what it was like."
And she cried.
She had not cried. Not when her father died, with her hand in his and his finger tapping the stairs on her palm, one, two, three, all the way to fourteen, and his other hand shut tight on whatever it was holding, and Corin's gray hand laid over it. Not when she said, that's the landing, Father, you can stop now. Not when he stopped. Not on the dyke road in the snow or in the fens or on the drove road or at Haverstock in front of the cross with all the names. She had not cried once. She had been too busy. Too frightened. Too angry. There had always been a next thing.
Now there was no next thing.
There was only a gravel shelf at the edge of the thorns, and the blue hills, and the sun going down the south, and a man beside her who did not remember her at all telling her that her father had loved her like the sea in a harbor.
She cried the way she had not cried since she was a little girl. Not quietly. Not prettily. Not like a Thorne. Her face crumpled up and her shoulders shook and the sound came out of her in great ugly gulps, and she could not stop it, and she did not try. She stood there on the gravel with her bare hands over her face and the tears running out between her fingers and down her wrists into her sleeves, and she cried for him. For the green lamp and the moon clock and the leather chairs. For the study with the curtains shut. For the vault on the Hill and the box on the shelf beside her mother. For Rowan in the front pew with no one beside him. For the thing her father had said to her in the dark of the vault when she was small, to make her not afraid, that she did not have anymore and never would.
She cried for a long time.
Corin did not say anything. He did not tell her it was all right. He did not tell her to stop. He stood beside her and let her cry, the way you let rain fall.
Then, when the worst of it had gone by, and she was standing there with her face wet and her breath catching and her hands hanging at her sides again, he moved.
He shifted the crutch to his right side, under his right arm. And he held out his left hand to her. Gray, like the right.
He held it out sideways, between them, low, palm up. The way you might hold out a hand to a frightened animal, so as not to startle it. In the low gold light of the afternoon she could see it clearly. The gray skin, smooth and dull, like a stone in a riverbed. The black fingertips. The way the fingers did not quite straighten, because the gray had stiffened them. It was not a pretty hand. It was a hand that had taken things out of people for years and years, and had paid for every one.
It was the hand that had lain over her father's shut hand, at the end.
She looked at it.
She thought of the little girl by the fire at Thistle Ford, with her two fair plaits, who had touched his gray palm and said it was cold, like a stone in the river.
Then she put her bare hand in it.
It was cold. The little girl had been right. Cold and smooth and dry, like a stone. But his fingers closed round hers. Slowly. Stiffly. Not tight. Just enough.
And under the cold, deep down, very faint, there was warmth.
They stood there, the two of them, hand in hand, facing south. Neither of them said anything more. There was nothing more to say. The sun went on going down the sky, and the shadows of the thorn bushes stretched out long and blue across the gravel, and the second bell after noon, far away in the city, on the Hill, rang and stopped, and rang and stopped, and then did not ring anymore.
And she held on.
Sticks
They heard the shouting before they got back to the tents.
It was children. A great many children, all shouting at once, high and shrill and wild, the way children shout at a fair when the bear comes out. And under the shouting, a sound Lyra knew at once, though she had not heard it in weeks. A hard flat crack, and another, and a scuffle of feet. Wood on wood.
She let go of Corin's hand.
She had held it all the way back from the gravel shelf, through the thorns, without either of them saying anything about it. Now she let it go, and wiped her face quickly with both palms, and pulled her gloves out of her pocket and put them on. Corin did not say anything about that either.
They came round the last tent into the open space by the big fire.
The whole camp was there. Or it seemed like it. Ashborn were standing all round the edge of the open ground in a ring, three and four deep, men and women and old ones and babies on hips, and in front of them, in a ragged shrieking front row, every child in Last Thorn. Some were sitting on their parents' shoulders. Some had climbed onto the bread racks. One had climbed onto the great heap of thorn wood by the fire and was standing on the top of it, waving both arms, while a woman shouted at him to get down.
And in the middle of the ring, on the bare beaten earth, Oren and Arran were fighting with sticks.
They were long sticks. Thorn wood, Lyra thought, stripped of its spines and its bark, as thick as a wrist and as long as a sword and a half. Each of them held one in both hands, the way you might hold a heavy two-handed blade. Oren had taken off his coat and was in his shirt, with the sleeves rolled up over his big forearms, and his gray beard was full of dust, and he was breathing hard, steam going up off him in the cold. Arran had taken off his fur and his hide tunic both, and was fighting bare to the waist, thin and brown and all ribs, with the long plait of his hair flying out behind him as he moved.
And he moved. Saints, he moved. He was quick. Quicker than anyone Lyra had seen, except perhaps the masters at the fencing school, in the old days. He did not stand still for a breath. He was always going, round and round Oren, light on the balls of his feet, in and out, darting, spinning, his stick whirling. He laughed while he did it. His bark of a laugh, over and over, every time he went in.
Oren did not move much at all.
He stood in the middle, with his feet planted wide, and turned. That was all. He turned to face Arran, wherever Arran went. Slowly. Heavily. Like a door swinging on a hinge. And every time Arran came in, whirling, the end of Oren's stick was there. Not fast. It did not look fast. It looked, if anything, slow and lazy. But it was always there, exactly where Arran's stick was going to be, a breath before Arran's stick got there.
Crack.
Arran went in low. Oren's stick went down and met his.
Crack.
Arran spun and came in high. Oren's stick came up.
Crack. Crack.
And then Oren took one step. Just one, forward, sideways, short and quick and nothing like the slow turning of before. And his stick went in under Arran's, and up, and Arran's stick went spinning out of his hands into the air and came down in the crowd, and the children shrieked and scattered, and the end of Oren's stick was resting, very lightly, on the middle of Arran's bare brown chest.
The crowd roared.
Arran stood there with his arms spread out and his chest going up and down under the end of the stick. Then he threw his head back and laughed so loud that the goats in the pen began to bleat.
"Three!" shouted a child somewhere. "That's three!"
"Three!" shouted all the other children.
Lyra found Kestrel standing at the edge of the ring beside her. She had not seen her come. Kestrel was watching the two men with her arms folded and no expression on her face at all.
"How long have they been at it?" said Lyra.
"Since the sun was there." Kestrel tipped her head at the sky, a little way east of where the sun stood now. "Arran asked him. Arran asks everyone. He has never lost to anyone at Last Thorn since he was fifteen." A pause. "He has lost three times now."
One of the children brought Arran's stick back to him. He took it, and swung it round his head twice, and grinned at Oren, and said something Lyra did not hear. Oren grunted. Then he wiped his face with his rolled-up sleeve, and settled his feet again, and lifted his stick.
They went again.
Lyra watched Oren.
She had seen him fight many times. With a sword. With his fists. Once, on the canal path, with a broken oar. She knew how he moved. She had grown up watching him in the yard at Crown Walk, drilling the house guards in the mornings while she watched from the schoolroom window instead of doing her sums. She knew the shape of him in a fight the way she knew the shape of her own hand.
And so she saw it.
Arran came in. Fast and laughing, the stick whirling. Low, then high, then low again, then a spin. Oren turned, and turned, and the end of his stick was there, and there, and there.
And then it was not.
Only for a breath. Only by a hand's width. Arran came in high, and Oren's stick came up to meet his, the way it had a hundred times, and it came up a little slow. A little short. And Arran's stick slid past it and caught Oren across the side of the ribs with a crack that made the whole crowd gasp.
Oren staggered. He went down on one knee. He dropped his stick.
And the crowd went mad.
The children screamed. The grown ones shouted. The boy on top of the wood heap jumped up and down until the heap began to slide and he slid down with it, shrieking. Arran stood over Oren with his stick held up over his head in both hands, and his face split in the widest grin Lyra had ever seen on a human being, and he shouted something in the round Ashborn speech, and the whole camp shouted it back.
Oren knelt on the ground with one hand pressed to his ribs, and shook his head slowly, like a bull that has been hit, and then looked up at Arran and laughed. A real laugh. Big and rough and deep, out of his belly.
"Saints," he said. "You've got me. Help an old man up, will you."
Arran threw the stick away and held out both hands and pulled him up, and they stood there in the middle of the ring with their hands on each other's shoulders, laughing, the tall thin brown one and the big gray-bearded one, with steam going up off both of them into the cold air.
Lyra watched Oren's face.
And for one moment, over Arran's shoulder, Oren's eyes found hers in the crowd.
He did not wink. He did not smile. Nothing on his face changed at all. He only looked at her, for a breath, steady and calm, with his eyes saying, plainly, the way they had said things to her across the yard at Crown Walk when she was eight years old and he had let her win at something: Don't you dare.
Then he looked away, and clapped Arran on the back, and went to get his coat.
Lyra looked at Kestrel.
Kestrel was still standing with her arms folded, watching the two men walk away together through the crowd. Her face had not changed either. But Lyra thought she had seen it too. She thought Kestrel saw most things.
"He let him win," Lyra said, very low.
Kestrel did not answer. But after a moment she said, "Arran will be happy for a month."
And then, a little later, in the same flat voice, she said, "We think the camp has decided something."
Lyra looked round.
The crowd was breaking up. But it was not going away. It was going to Oren. The children first, running, swarming round him as he pulled on his coat, grabbing at his hands and his sleeves and the hem of the coat, shouting at him, asking him things. Then the grown ones. A man came and slapped him on the back. A woman came and pressed a cup of something hot into his hands. An old man came and stood in front of him and looked up at him for a long time and then touched the gray line on his own face with two fingers, forehead to nose, and nodded, and went away. The goat that had followed Oren all last night had come out of nowhere and was butting at his knees.
Oren stood in the middle of all of it with the cup in his hands and his coat half on and a child hanging off each arm, looking down at them all with an expression of the purest bewilderment Lyra had ever seen on his face.
"What have I done?" he said, to nobody in particular.
Nobody answered him.
But Lyra knew. They had decided that they loved him.
